newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak Q1 GDP slows, forecast to ease further.
newsitem.headline: Slovak Q1 GDP slows, forecast to ease further.

text.p: Slovak real GDP growth, as expected, slowed in the first quarter of 1997, and analysts said they saw little room for any significant acceleration of the economic growth later in the year.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) on Wednesday said GDP for the first three months of the year grew 5.1 percent, year-on-year, after a 7.3 percent real GDP growth rate for the same period in 1996.

"This (first quarter) figure is surprisingly good given the current economic situation in Slovakia, but I think GDP will continue to slow down throughout the year," said Vladimir Kuklis, an analyst at Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.
SUSR said its estimate for GDP growth for the first half of this year was between 5.7 and 6.3 percent, before slowing down to 5.6 percent for the full year.
Kuklis said the biggest danger to the economy was the turbulent situation on the local money market.
The central bank has choked off liquidity to support the crown, but in turn pushed interest rates to levels of above 30 percent over the past three weeks.
The high rates are hitting Slovak companies hard since they often draw short- and medium-term crown credits to refinance their activities and investments.
"The economy will simply feel the negative effect of such high rates...the full year GDP will probably not even exceed five percent," Kuklis said.
Some analysts expect GDP growth to speed up slightly in the second quarter, due to an acceleration in foreign demand and industrial and construction output in April.
Slovak exports rose 16.7 percent year-on-year in the January-April period of this year while industrial production and construction output increased by 9.0 and 10.8 percent, respectively, in April.

"Given these factors, GDP should grow at a slightly faster pace in the second quarter," said Martin Barto, an analyst at ING Barings. He added that the first half GDP growth could be at around 5.7 percent.

Many analysts said the most worrying factor in Slovakia's economic develpoment in the first quarter was a radical increase in wages which could spark inflationary pressures and boost Slovakia's foreign indebteness.
The average monthly wage rose to 8,198 crowns in the first quarter of 1997, a real year-on-year increase of 8.1 percent.
"This is really alarming...this economy just cannot afford such an increase in wages compared to economic growth," Barto said. "This money is just not backed by real production (increases)."
